definition: To make up for a wrong you have done, or for your guilt, by doing something to set it right.
example: She tried to expiate her rudeness at dinner by writing each guest a sincere apology.
nuance: The wrongdoer expiates by paying off guilt through action; someone else absolves by forgiving, and expatiate means to talk at length.
prompt: A teammate who skipped practice before a big game wants to make up for letting the team down.
options: To expiate skipping practice, she volunteered to coach the younger players all week.
During the team meeting, she began to expiate at length on her favorite plays.
The coach chose to expiate her, announcing that the missed practice was forgiven.
To expiate skipping one practice, she cheerfully skipped the next two sessions as well.
reasons: Doing extra work for the team is a concrete way to pay off her guilt.
Talking on and on about a topic is expatiating, a look-alike with an unrelated meaning.
Forgiving someone else is absolving; only the person at fault can make amends.
Repeating the offense adds to her guilt instead of repairing it.

practice.prompt: A neighbor carelessly backed a wheelbarrow into the shared garden fence and knocked a section down.
options: He began to expiate about fence materials until the neighbors drifted away.
The old fence was so weak that it seemed ready to expiate on its own.
He tried to expiate his carelessness by rebuilding the fence himself over the weekend.
He tried to expiate his carelessness by blaming the wind and refusing to discuss it further.
reasons: Lecturing at length confuses the word with expatiate.
A fence wearing out or expiring is not a person making amends for a wrong.
Fixing the harm he caused is a real act of making amends.
Denying responsibility does nothing to set the wrong right.
